domain: Comparative Law / Legal Pluralism / Constitutional Theory
topic_summary: Analysis of India's parallel personal-law regime where Hindu, Muslim, Christian, Parsi, and secular marriage/family law systems operate simultaneously within one constitutional state. The kernel contest is whether 'marriage and family law authority' is one commitment read multiple ways or multiple incoherent kernels coexisting without synthesis.

key_entities: Hindu Marriage Act 1955 (codified Hindu personal law)
Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act 1937 (uncodified religious law)
Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act 1936 (community-specific codification)
Supreme Court of India (constitutional arbiter; UCC jurisdiction)
key_tensions: Religious community autonomy vs uniform citizenship rights (personal law systems vs UCC advocates)
Codified vs uncodified authority (Hindu/Christian/Parsi statutes vs Muslim Shariat interpretation)
Constitutional secularism vs legal pluralism (Article 44 directive vs Article 25-28 religious freedom)

axes.human_readable: Marriage and Family Law Authority (Contested Kernel)
axes.structural_delta: The shared commitment that some authority legitimately adjudicates marriage validity, divorce terms, inheritance, and custody — but different communities read this commitment through incompatible interpretive frameworks
axes.primary_observable: Which court/authority has jurisdiction over a marriage dispute; which substantive rules apply; whether parties can exit to another regime
axes.selection_reason: Core kernel with 5 distinct readings; highest centrality; upstream to all other axes

axes.structural_delta: Differential costs of switching between personal law regimes via conversion, Special Marriage Act opt-in, or jurisdictional forum-shopping
axes.primary_observable: Conversion rates; Special Marriage Act usage by community; court forum selection patterns
axes.selection_reason: Structurally independent from kernel (different observable: mobility costs not authority grounding); downstream synthesis of regime interaction effects

axes.structural_delta: Differential rights for women in divorce, maintenance, custody, and inheritance depending on which personal law applies
axes.primary_observable: Comparative legal entitlements by regime (e.g., triple talaq vs Hindu Maintenance Act); Supreme Court gender justice interventions
axes.selection_reason: Independent observable (substantive rights not authority structure); high epsilon; captures extractive dimension of pluralism

omegas.description: Is the Uniform Civil Code (Article 44) a dormant constitutional mandate that will eventually collapse the kernel, or is coexistence the stable equilibrium? Shah Bano (1985) and triple talaq ban (2017) suggest incremental convergence, but political economy of minority appeasement may sustain pluralism indefinitely.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 3 (Beneficiary Scan) + constitutional directive analysis

omegas.description: Scheduled Tribes under Article 244/Fifth Schedule operate customary law outside all five regimes. Is this a sixth reading or a separate kernel? Absence suggests personal law analysis is incomplete without tribal legal pluralism.

Post-Navtej Singh Johar (2018 decriminalization), same-sex couples have no access to any personal law regime. Does this reveal that all five readings share a heteronormative axiom, collapsing the kernel into one reading with surface variation?
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 1 (Operational Medium) + LGBTQ+ rights jurisprudence gap

omegas.description: Cross-border marriages and NRI divorces create jurisdictional conflicts where Indian personal law collides with foreign civil codes. Does this expose the kernel as territorially bounded rather than universally contested?

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. Five-reading decomposition reflects actual legal regime structure. Exit_cost_structure and gender_rights_variance pass §3 independence test (different observables, different epsilon sources). Tribal customary law and same-sex marriage gaps documented as omegas rather than forcing sixth/seventh readings.

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The shared commitment that some legitimate authority adjudicates the validity of marriage, terms of divorce, inheritance rights, and child custody — but the grounding of that authority (scriptural, statutory, customary, contractual) and the substantive rules it enforces differ radically across communities
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Hindu/Christian/Parsi: Parliamentary statute interpreted by secular courts. Muslim: Shariat as interpreted by community qazis/ulema with limited judicial review. Secular: Contract law enforced by civil courts. All regimes claim constitutional legitimacy under Articles 25-28 (religious freedom) vs Article 44 (UCC directive).

readings.commitment: Marriage authority derives from parliamentary codification of dharmashastra principles, enforced by secular courts with constitutional override
readings.authority_grounding: Statutory positivism with Hindu cultural substrate; Hindu Marriage Act 1955 as authoritative text
readings.expected_structural_delta: Codified rules; judicial enforcement; gender reforms via amendment (e.g., 1976 divorce grounds expansion); moderate exit costs to secular regime

readings.commitment: Marriage authority derives from divine revelation (Quran/Hadith) as interpreted by Islamic jurisprudence, with minimal state interference
readings.authority_grounding: Religious textualism; ulema/qazi interpretation; 1937 Shariat Act as protective shield against state codification
readings.expected_structural_delta: Uncodified rules; community enforcement; high gender asymmetry (triple talaq pre-2017, polygamy, unequal inheritance); high exit costs for women

readings.commitment: Marriage authority derives from ecclesiastical tradition as codified by colonial statute, enforced by secular courts
readings.authority_grounding: Hybrid: Church canon law filtered through 1872 colonial legislation; statutory text as authoritative
readings.expected_structural_delta: Codified but archaic (no divorce until 2001 amendment); judicial enforcement; moderate gender asymmetry; moderate exit costs

readings.commitment: Marriage authority derives from Zoroastrian community norms as codified by community-specific statute
readings.authority_grounding: Ethno-religious community self-governance; 1936 Parsi Marriage Act as authoritative; judicial enforcement
readings.expected_structural_delta: Codified; judicial enforcement; low gender asymmetry; endogamy enforcement (non-Parsi spouse loses community status); low exit costs to secular regime

readings.commitment: Marriage authority derives from individual consent formalized as civil contract under secular law, independent of religious identity
readings.authority_grounding: Liberal contractualism; Special Marriage Act 1954 as opt-in alternative; purely judicial enforcement
readings.expected_structural_delta: Fully codified; no religious content; gender-neutral rules; inter-faith marriage enabled; social stigma as informal exit cost

axiom_contradictions.basis: Shariat reading holds divine law as non-negotiable and superior to state law; secular reading holds individual consent as sole legitimate basis for marriage authority. No single framework can hold both axioms — accepting divine law supremacy requires rejecting consent-based legitimacy, and vice versa.

Hindu reading accepts parliamentary sovereignty to reform religious law via statute (1955 Act overrode polygamy, reformed divorce); Muslim reading rejects state authority to codify or reform Shariat. No framework holds both — accepting legislative reform power requires rejecting divine law immunity from state revision.

Parsi reading grounds authority in ethno-religious community membership (endogamy enforcement, loss of status for out-marriage); secular reading grounds authority in individual choice independent of community. No framework holds both — accepting community-membership-as-authority requires rejecting individual-choice-as-sole-basis.
